comparison: Perfect alignment on SNP distance data (C30-C32, C122-C125). Both evaluations support the close genetic relationships between cattle and human isolates. OpenEval provides detailed interpretation of bimodal distribution suggesting imported vs. local populations, while peer reviewers praised the combined sampling approach and phylogenetic quality without specific critique.

Perfect alignment on outbreak analysis (C62-C65). Both evaluations support the link between LPLs and major outbreaks. OpenEval notes that non-LPL outbreaks demonstrate LPLs don't account for all activity, while peer reviewers accepted this as evidence of ongoing cattle involvement in transmission.

Strong alignment on STEC background and transmission routes (C7-C18). Both evaluations support these well-cited contextual claims. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of how claims distinguish established knowledge from uncertainty, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted this standard epidemiological background.

Strong alignment on epidemiological context (C1-C6). Both evaluations support the framing of high-incidence regions and knowledge gaps. OpenEval explicitly notes appropriate acknowledgment of surveillance limitations, while peer reviewers accepted the study's motivating premise about understanding local transmission.

Strong alignment on local evolution evidence (C66-C70, C82-C86). Both evaluations support that LPLs are locally evolved rather than imported. OpenEval raises concern about sampling bias potentially affecting global export conclusions, while peer reviewers accepted the local evolution narrative as part of high-quality analysis without this caveat.

Strong alignment on phylogenetic characterization (C21-C26). Both evaluations support the dramatic clade G(vi) enrichment in Alberta and toxin profile differences. OpenEval provides quantitative detail on enrichment percentages, while peer reviewers described this as foundational 'solid evidence' for the study.

Strong alignment on LPL identification and characteristics (C43-C47, C50-C51, C79-C81, C117). Both evaluations support the LPL findings as a major contribution. OpenEval critiques the arbitrary 30 SNP threshold and calls for sensitivity analysis, while peer reviewers accepted the methodology without questioning threshold selection.

Strong alignment on cattle-to-human transmission estimates (C33, C35, C39-C41, C76, C116). Both evaluations strongly support this central quantitative finding. OpenEval notes potential underestimation due to sampling strategy, while peer reviewers explicitly stated the evidence is 'solid' without methodological concerns.

Strong alignment on LPL persistence and virulence shift (C56-C57, C90-C91, C118). Both evaluations support the temporal findings and stx2a increase. OpenEval emphasizes public health concern and notes unexplained mechanism, while peer reviewers highlighted this as a key finding without questioning causation.

Alignment on study novelty and implications (C119-C121). Both evaluations support the study's contributions. OpenEval expresses concern that causality is not established and comparison to lower-incidence regions is lacking, while peer reviewers endorsed public health implications through positive overall assessment without these reservations.

Alignment on literature contextualization (C99-C107). Both evaluations support how the study integrates with existing literature on pathogen persistence. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of comparisons and acknowledgment of uncertainties, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted this as part of high-quality discussion.

Alignment on contextual STEC information (C89, C92-C98). Both evaluations support these cited background claims. OpenEval notes they effectively contextualize findings, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted them as part of the overall high-quality study without specific comment.

Partial overlap on temporal and population parameters (C34, C36-C38). Both evaluations support these technical estimates. OpenEval assesses parameters as within reasonable ranges, while peer reviewers accepted phylogenetic analyses as high quality without detailed parameter critique.

Partial overlap on virulence profiles (C58-C61). Both evaluations support the virulence shift findings. OpenEval focuses on quantitative changes and emergence patterns, while peer reviewers emphasized the shift to stx2a-only strains as a key contribution.

Partial overlap on strain characterization (C71-C74). Both evaluations support genetic distance data distinguishing imported from local strains. OpenEval provides detailed interpretation, while peer reviewers accepted this as part of comprehensive well-thought-through analysis.

Partial overlap on toxin profiles (C27-C29). Both evaluations support virulence characterization data. OpenEval treats these as descriptive phylogenetic findings, while peer reviewers incorporated them into the broader virulence shift narrative.

Partial overlap on dating estimates (C77-C78). Both evaluations support temporal estimates. OpenEval notes consistency with prior work, while peer reviewers accepted these as part of high-quality phylogenetic analysis supporting the evolutionary narrative.

Minimal overlap on sensitivity analysis (C113). Both evaluations support the robustness checks. OpenEval uses balanced sampling results to suggest potential underestimation in primary analysis, while peer reviewers treated sensitivity analyses as strengthening conclusions.

Minimal overlap on control strategies (C109-C111). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting C111's ring vaccination suggestion is speculative without supporting data. Peer reviewers did not specifically challenge these claims, accepting them as part of the overall discussion.

Minimal overlap on phylogenetic clustering (C48-C49). Both evaluations support temporal and host inference patterns. OpenEval treats these as evidence for LPL identification robustness, while peer reviewers accepted them as supporting local evolution within Alberta.

Minimal overlap on study limitations (C112, C114-C115). Both evaluations support these contextual claims. OpenEval explicitly assesses how limitations are addressed, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted them through positive overall assessment.

Minimal overlap on cattle proximity and incidence (C19-C20). Both evaluations support these claims linking cattle proximity to disease risk. OpenEval notes they provide rationale for the study's focus, while peer reviewers accepted the motivating premise.

Minimal overlap on transient strain characteristics (C52-C53). Both evaluations support characterization of non-LPL strains. OpenEval treats these as supporting data on strain origins, while peer reviewers accepted them as part of comprehensive analysis.

Minimal overlap on LPL virulence (C54-C55). Both evaluations support virulence data. OpenEval groups these with LPL characteristics, while peer reviewers incorporated them into the virulence shift narrative.

Minimal overlap on sampling robustness (C42). Both evaluations support the balanced sampling analysis. OpenEval notes this suggests potential underestimation in primary analysis, while peer reviewers found sensitivity analyses acceptable and strengthening.

Minimal overlap on novelty claims (C75, C108). Both evaluations support the study's novel contributions. OpenEval provides specific assessment of quantitative transmission estimates, while peer reviewers implicitly endorsed novelty through positive overall evaluation.

Minimal overlap on LPL definition parameter (C47). Both evaluations support the methodology. OpenEval critiques arbitrary threshold selection, while peer reviewers accepted the approach through acknowledgment of authors' diligence in addressing comments.
